Maximum Likelihood Computation using Homomorphic Computation

Balasubramanian Narasimhan

2026-06-26

Source: vignettes/homomorphing.Rmd
homomorphing.Rmd

Introduction

We present a toy example of a homomorphic computation involving maximum likelihood estimation.

Consider the following data motivated by an example from the mle function in the stats4 R package: we wish to estimate λ\lambda, the Poisson parameter λ\lambda for randomly generated count data y below:

library(stats4)
set.seed(17822)
y <- rpois(n = 40, lambda=10)
# Easy one-dimensional MLE:
nLL <- function(lambda) -sum(stats::dpois(y, lambda, log = TRUE))
fit0 <- mle(nLL, start = list(lambda = 5), nobs = NROW(y))

The function nLL is the negative log-likelihood of the data and the function mle computes the maximum likelihood estimate that can be printed out.

summary(fit0)
## Maximum likelihood estimation
## 
## Call:
## mle(minuslogl = nLL, start = list(lambda = 5), nobs = NROW(y))
## 
## Coefficients:
##        Estimate Std. Error
## lambda    9.175  0.4789311
## 
## -2 log L: 199.5328
logLik(fit0)
## 'log Lik.' -99.76641 (df=1)

Distributed Computation

Assume now that the data y is distributed between three sites, none of whom want to share actual data among each other or even with a master computation process. They wish to keep their data secret but are willing, together, to provide the sum of their local negative log-likelihoods. They need to do this in a way so that the master process will not be able to associate the contribution to the likelihood from each site. To simulate this, let’s partition the data y as follows.

y1 <- y[1:20]
y2 <- y[21:27]
y3 <- y[28:40]

The overall likelihood function l(λ)l(\lambda) for the entire data is therefore the sum of the likelihoods at each site: l(λ)=l1(λ)+l2(λ)+l3(λ).l(\lambda) = l_1(\lambda)+l_2(\lambda)+l_3(\lambda). How can this likelihood be computed while maintaining privacy?

Assuming that every site including the master has access to a homomorphic computation library such as homomorpheR, the likelihood can be computed in a privacy-preserving manner using the following scheme. We use E(x)E(x) and D(x)D(x) to denote the encrypted and decrypted values of xx respectively.

  1. Master generates a public/private key pair. Master distributes the public key to all sites. (The private key is not distributed and kept only by the master.)
  2. Master generates a random offset rr to obfuscate the intial likelihood.
  3. Master sends E(r)E(r) and a guess λ0\lambda_0 to site 1. Note that λ\lambda is not encrypted.
  4. Site 1 computes l1=l(λ0,y1)l_1 = l(\lambda_0, y_1), the local likelihood for local data y1y_1 using parameter λ0\lambda_0. It then sends on λ0\lambda_0 and E(r)+E(l1)E(r) + E(l_1) to site 2.
  5. Site 2 computes l2=l(λ0,y2)l_2 = l(\lambda_0, y_2), the local likelihood for local data y2y_2 using parameter λ0\lambda_0. It then sends on λ0\lambda_0 and E(r)+E(l1)+E(l2)E(r) + E(l_1) + E(l_2) to site 3.
  6. Site 3 computes l3=l(λ0,y3)l_3 = l(\lambda_0, y_3), the local likelihood for local data y3y_3 using parameter λ0\lambda_0. It then sends on E(r)+E(l1)+E(l2)+E(l3)E(r) + E(l_1) + E(l_2) + E(l_3) back to master.
  7. Master retrieves E(r)+E(l1)+E(l2)+E(l3)E(r) + E(l_1) + E(l_2) + E(l_3) which, due to the homomorphism, is exactly E(r+l1+l2+l3)=E(r+l).E(r+l_1+l_2+l_3) = E(r+l). So the master computes D(E(r+l))−rD(E(r+l)) - r to obtain the value of the overall likelihood at λ0\lambda_0.
  8. Master updates λ0\lambda_0 with a new guess λ1\lambda_1 and repeats steps 1-5. This process is iterated to convergence. For added security, even steps 0-5 can be repeated, at additional computational cost.

This is pictorially shown below.

Round robin scheme

Implementation

The above implementation assumes that the encryption and decryption can happen with real numbers which is not the actual situation. Instead, we use rational approximations using a large denominator, 22562^{256}, say. In the future, of course, we need to build an actual library is built with rigorous algorithms guaranteeing precision and overflow/undeflow detection. For now, this is just an ad hoc implementation.

Also, since we are only using homomorphic additive properties, a partial homomorphic scheme such as the Paillier Encryption system will be sufficient for our computations.

The package exports a small actor surface — Site, Master, and the helpers make_site(), make_master(), round_robin_chain(), run_round_robin() — that captures the round-robin protocol once and lets each application supply its own per-site summary function.

The per-site negative log-likelihood is just an ordinary R function of (data, theta). We write it out and hand it to the constructor:

library(homomorpheR)

local_nll <- function(data, lambda) {
    -sum(stats::dpois(data, lambda, log = TRUE))
}

1. Generate a key pair 

keys <- paillier_keypair(modulus_bits = 1024)

2. Build sites and master, wire the chain 

site1  <- make_site("Site 1", data = y1, local_fn = local_nll)
site2  <- make_site("Site 2", data = y2, local_fn = local_nll)
site3  <- make_site("Site 3", data = y3, local_fn = local_nll)
master <- make_master("Master", keypair = keys)
round_robin_chain(master, list(site1, site2, site3))

round_robin_chain() wires master -> site1 -> site2 -> site3 -> master and broadcasts the public key to every site.

3. Perform the likelihood estimation 

fit1 <- mle(function(lambda) run_round_robin(master, lambda),
            start = list(lambda = 5))

Print the summary.

summary(fit1)
## Maximum likelihood estimation
## 
## Call:
## mle(minuslogl = function(lambda) run_round_robin(master, lambda), 
##     start = list(lambda = 5))
## 
## Coefficients:
##        Estimate Std. Error
## lambda    9.175  0.4789307
## 
## -2 log L: 199.5328
logLik(fit1)
## 'log Lik.' -99.76641 (df=1)

The results should be the same as above.

Applications via distcomp and opencpu

One can imagine these sort of computations being constructed within the framework described the R package distcomp where the sites are opencpu servers and there is a master process executing the computation. Much work remains to be done to make this work in a seamless manner; however, as this proof-of-concept example shows, the technical hurdles are quite surmountable.

CAVEAT

This is an initial proof-of-concept implementation that has to substantially improved for real-world use. You’ve been warned.
